speechtext:
That is very easy to
answer, and I will come to that. I do not mind interruptions, I welcome them. I might just as well say now that this charter, as I see it, is a canal charter and nothing else. It is primarily a canal charter with certain rights and obligations incidental thereto. The primary intent of this charter is the construction of a canal before anything else can be done. I stand by that and by that alone, and my own legal training and understanding and my common sense tell me, after having read the charter, as I will do again later, that it is a charter for the construction of a canal, and the development of the surplus power resulting therefrom. I will read the section dealing with that matter later.
I am asked if anybody in the city is against the canal. I have before me an absolutely independent newspaper, neither Grit nor Tory, owing allegiance to no party, a paper which fought me in some elections and I propose to read to the House what this French-Canadian paper in the city of Ottawa, Le Droit, said in connection with the Georgian bay canal at Ottawa. I give that paper credit for expressing its opinion courageously and fearlessly. On March 8, 1927, Le Droit published the following:
The Georgian Bay Canal Company requests, for the fourteenth time since its inception, the renewal of its charter.
It was an excellent opportunity to re-open the discussion on the advantages which the country might derive from the construction of this essentially Canadian waterway, and the opportunity has not been allow'ed to slip by, seeing that since a week and a half it is the fourth time that the subject has been debated. A remarkable feature: the Tories, those haling from Ontario especially, condemn the project as being far less advantageous than that of dredging the St. Lawrence in order to reach the great lakes by way of the Welland canal, and upon which the government has unwisely invested as much as $75,000,000.
By this attitude, these Tories shatter the traditions of their party. In fact, if we refer back to Sir John Macdonald-
They tell me that in the time of Sir John Macdonald the question of power was not discussed. In 1898 a Senate committee, charged with investigating these conditions, reported as follows:
Furthermore your committee are unanimously of the opinion that the development and use of the enormous water-power along the route for electrical purposes in the mining and smelting of iron and other ores, which are so abundant in the Ottawa valley, and which cannot now be

Georgian Bay Canal Company
developed by reason of the want of cheap communication and transportation, would of itself alone warrant the construction of the canal.
Now, Mr. Speaker, could anybody in the House say that these statesmen lacked forethought and vision when they made this report^ Now we proceed with the citation from Le Droit:
-if we refer back to Sir John Macdonald, we find that he made a statement of this kind: "The Ottawa canal and the Pacific railway must be constructed and no voice should be raised against the great national work which would open the western states and colonies to the seaboard".
It is just exactly the opposite of what was advocated yesterday afternoon by General Ross of Kingstou, who wished to see the Georgian bay canal doomed because it -would compete with the railways. Much later-we come to the views held by Sir Alexander Mackenzie who, in 1876, declared himself irrevocably in favour of this canal-Sir Robert Borden, in 1914, at the time he was Prime Minister, stated: "Our aim is to retain Canadian trade over Canadian routes and to follow, as much as possible, the policy which consists in having this trade move from east to west".
These three Conservative opinions suffice to prove that the Tory party, up to recent times at least, were in favour of the dredging of the Ottawa, the Mattawa and the French rivers, in preference to that of the St. Lawrence.
The late Paul-Emile Lamarche, who died at the age of thirty-seven after a political career the usefulness of which was in inverse ratio to its duration, in February 1914, on the floor of the House expressed the view which all true Canadians should to-day study in its bearings in order to remain permanently Canadian. We advise this same study to those who are not enough Canadians and who would like to become more so. Mr. Lamarche. after having disproved clearly all the objections which were then brought to bear against the construction of the Georgian bay canal, faces the question squarely and shows the advantages which would result from this enterprise and which the interests of Canada necessarily require. "The Georgian bay canal scheme", he stated then, "should include among its most enthusiastic supporters all those who not only endorse but also sincerely believe in the motto: Canada for the Canadians!" The whole of his magnificent speech is permeated with this patriotic motto and those pages are not only a homage to the youthful orator who conceived them, but to the Canadian race which gave Canada such a statesman.
It is more and more evident that these opponents of this essentially Canadian water route are the victims of a narrow patriotism, a sectional patriotism, perhaps also the victims of large foreign interests. For, after all, if the Americans did not find the dredging of the St. Lawrence to their advantage, they would not support it so willingly. It is not among our neighbours to the south that practical philanthropy exists the most.

While we are at it, let us consider this section, because the whole of the argument turns upon its interpretation. When this charter was originally granted it was obtained for the purpose of constructing a canal; if Hansard is looked through the fact will be revealed that there was no discussion as to the desire of those promoting this bill simply to produce power and forego the construction of a canal. But power in those days was not an unknown quantity; power was not something out of the vision of those who granted this charter. I have just read an extract from the report of the Senate committee of 1898, the charter having been granted in 1894, and that committee considered the question of power to be of tremendous importance. But no matter how great or how important that power may be the charter must be read in the light of day and according to its exact wording; one must place an interpretation on the words contained therein, and by no construction can anyone say that the primary motive of this charter was the securing of power. So much has public opinion been distorted in this House, willingly in certain quarters and innocently in others, that the hon. member
for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) on February 16 asked for a return of the House in these terms:
For a copy of all applications, letters, reports, orders in council, correspondence and all other communications between the government and any other person or persons as to the renewal of charters or agreements, or extension of the same, regarding the Ottawa, Montreal and Georgian Bay Canal Company, for power and navigation rights on the Ottawa river.
There must have been some idea in the mind of the hon. member that some negotiations were proceeding for the purpose of securing the power alone, but what did he find? The return came down and there was not a tittle of evidence or a scrap of paper of any kind to show that at any time this corporation had expressed a desire to forego the canal rights and substitute therefor the power rights. The primary idea of this company was to build a canal, and that is the idea to-day.
I am an Ontario man and believe in public ownership; I have the greatest respect for the memory of Sir Adam Beck, and it is due to his genius and his perspicacity and sense of business that this system of public ownership was developed in Ontario. But I cannot say as much for those who have succeeded him. This charter was granted in 1894; section 8 (g) which I have just quoted was included in the bill until 1912, when Sir Adam Beck, seeing into the future, knowing the possibilities of hydraulic power in Ontario and looking to the future needs of the people of Ontario, saw that this charter of 1894 granted too many powers and rights in connection with the development of hydraulic power. He came to Ottawa and appeared before the committee which, Sir, shows the necessity of having a matter of this kind referred to a committee. When Sir Adam Beck appeared before that committee the matter was thoroughly threshed out and discussed, and what happened? The company agreed that its primary intention was the construction of a canal and nothing else, and they also agreed to the adoption of this amending section which took away the vast! powers granted in 1894 under section 8 (g). Produce, lease and supply, or otherwise dispose of surplus hydraulic, electric and other kinds of power-

A canal must be constructed, after which that surplus may be dealt with.

To that question they gave this answer:
The irresponsibe operation of the power works proposed by the board, or indeed of any power works, however designed, that develop fully the power resources of any section of the river, would affect injuriously the water levels in the St. Lawrence river at and below Montreal; but it is feasible to operate these works under government supervision in such a manner that they will neither lower the summer levels in the lower river nor raise the winter and spring levels. With such control the improvements proposed will have no injurious effect whatever on the water levels oij the St. Lawrence at and below Montreal.
Then for the benefit of my friends from the province of Quebec I would like to quote a portion of a telegram sent by the secretary of the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company to the premier of the province of Quebec:
We draw your attention to the fact that the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company is compelled by its charter to safeguard the interests of navigation and to operate its works on the Ottawa river in the interests of navigation and in the interest of maintaining water levels in the Ottawa river, Montreal harbour and in the St. Lawrence at the best levels for navigation. Clearly, if the riparian owner's are permitted to develop power only on the Ottawa river their works will fall within the dictum of the international joint board and will injuriously affect the levels of the Montreal harbour and in the lower St. Lawrence. We appeal to you in the first place to support the interests of navigation, in the second place to prevent the erection of water-power works on the Ottawa river which will injuriously affect the water levels in the Montreal harbour and the lower St. Lawrence; in the third place to use your influence to defend the great vested interests of your province established in the trade of the harbour of Montreal and the lower St. Lawrence generally and in the shipping and general commerce which is entirely dependent upon the maintenance and the protection of water levels in that area.
I would warn my good friends in Ontario of the danger of disturbing the economic equilibrium of this province by furthering so easily the monopolistic development of power in one section only in order to draw to that section commercial enterprises, to the detriment of other portions of Ontario. We all know that because of the situation in Ontario, power is being given to the immediate vicinity of Toronto and Hamilton while all the other portions of the province, especially those to the north, are ignored..

Then I would just say a word to hon. gentlemen directly opposite, who are also interested in cheap means of transportation, in the development of our resources and in the national development of Canada. More than that, I appeal to them because I know their independence; I know they are affiliated with no party in this House; I know the sincerity of their tenets and the loyalty with which they are adhered to, and I do not want anyone to accuse me of just saying this because of the expediency of the moment. I have said it before; I say it now and I will say it again no matter when or where. But I say also that not only because of what I have submitted to the House but because of the speeches made by other hon. members in favour of this measure, there should now be in their minds enough doubt and uncertainty to defeat this amendment, to allow the second reading of this bill and to send it to a committee, there to meet whatever its fate may be. I do not believe my friends opposite would think of killing this billin the House without giving to its promoters a chance to submit their own arguments; I think in their honesty of purpose and in their loyalty to themselves they will send this bill to a committee of this House where all questions will be thoroughly ventilated. If the members of that committee find that what I have said to-day is not true-although I defy anyone to say so-if they find that there are any objectionable features in that charter which should be removed, with the consent of the promoters that might be done. But if it is there found that the charter is fundamentally wrong and that there is something absolutely reprehensible about it, they can do as they please, kill it outright or let it linger. I do say, however, that it is incumbent upon those hon. members as well as upon every other member of this House to make sure that a question of this kind should be referred to a committee.
I have just a few more words to add. After all, Mr. Speaker, I am not so much concerned about the building of this canal and the exploitation of power as I am concerned with a matter of much greater importance. It is true that the construction of this canal and the exploitation of these water-powers are of great importance to the economic welfare of this common country of ours, but that has more to do with the material side of things. When our early Canadian statesmen laid the foundations of our present national development, they did not do so in terms of

Georyian Bay Canal Company
dollars and cents. They did not do it in the terms of interest to this one or to that one, and the criticisms hurled at them were far in excess of the congratulations which they received. To-day the works of Cartier, Macdonald, Mackenzie and Laurier stand out in our national life as everlasting tributes to the memories of these great men. The preaching of the development of our internal trade, of the getting closer together of the various provinces in an endeavour to cure their common ills, of the blending together in the hearts and souls and minds of the Canadian people of their common desires and ambitions made feasible their materialization into those bonds and ties of steel that to-day bind together the provinces of this country, and have their origin in the construction of such works as that of the Canadian Pacific railway.
But that is not enough, we must not stop here. Much more needs to be done; much more can be done to bring closer together in one common spirit the various forces and elements of this country. Uttering this sentiment is good, preaching it is good also, but the furnishing of the means to achieve the desired end is better, and that can only be done by the construction and the maintenance of such works as the one under review, a work which will bring the component parts of this country into closer commercial relations and thereby to a better understanding and a rapid solution of their respective needs.

I wish to say, as some other gentlemen have said, that I have no personal interest in this matter. I have not been canvassed by anybody, and I have not been lobbied by anybody, either for this bill or against it. I have come to my conclusion in regard to the bill, and the manner in which it should be disposed of, entirely from my general knowledge of the subject, as well as from the provisions of the bill itself and the arguments which have been advanced in the House. It ought to be a matter of gratification to those who believe in public ownership to hear the expressions of opinion that have come from across the House, even if we cannot believe there is as complete unanimity as the speeches which have been made on that side would seem to indicate.
An hon. member from Toronto made the remark that the line of cleavage between those in favour of public ownership and those in favour of private ownership ran down the centre of the House. I think in that respect he is entirely wrong. It seems to me that if you tried to draw a line between those in favour of public and those in favour of private ownership, it would cross the House a great number of times in order to include or exclude the hon. members in one or the other of these two classes. I cannot understand how it could possibly include those who would defend the order in council of August 26th last, neither do I think it could include those who were elected in response' to the "whisper of death" campaign that was carried on in Montreal some years ago. While we have heard many declarations in favour of public ownership from the other side it seems to me that I could detect at times a somewhat different note, a note that was not just as completely devoted to the idea of public ownership. Tor instance we could detect the note of the assertion of provincial rights. That, it seems to me, was a thought far more prominent in the minds of some of the speakers than the idea of public ownership.
I wish to call attention to the speech that was made by the hon. member for Toronto Northeast (Mr. Young). I need not read the

Georgian Bay Canal (Tompany
passages from his speech where he emphasized his attachment to the idea of public ownership. Having done that-of course, with all the fervour that might characterize the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans), or the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) or the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth)-later on in his speech he said, speaking of the matter dealt with by the order in council of August 26th:
I repeat again, that the National hydro contract to which my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Glen) referred, was a contract approved by both the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
That is, he is intensely devoted to the * principle of public ownership, but when the government of Ontario sets its seal of approval upon a contract that violates all those principles, then his adhesion to the principle of public ownership goes by the board.
There is another need that seems to have been emphasized by some hon. gentlemen opposite, and that is the question of the St. Lawrence waterway. I have no doubt that-the matter of the deepening of the St. Lawrence had1 some place in the thoughts of my hon. friend from Fort William-

-for we know he is very greatly attached to that project. I am not going to find any fault with him for that, but in speaking of this matter the leader of the opposition used an argument that seemed to me to be absolutely fallacious. He contended it would not be wise for us to construct a waterway that might enter into competition with those other great lines of transportation that we have in mind-the St. Lawrence waterway, and I suppose he referred to our National Railways. I cannot see force in the argument that we should not allow a private right to compete with public enterprises, and the argument loses its force entirely when you remember that if the St. Lawrence waterway is ever constructed, the canals thereon will be thrown open to the public free, and we will not collect any revenue from them. Why then is it unwise for us to grant a charter in respect to a waterway coming into competition with another waterway from which the Dominion of Canada receives no revenue at all? If the argument is good against the Georgian bay canal scheme that it should not be allowed to enter into competition with our railways, the same argument is just as good against the St. Lawrence waterway. As a matter of fact that argument has been used against the construction of the 'St. Lawrence waterway-that it will enter into competition with our railways. I put these arguments

aside altogether, however, because I do not think they have any weight.
I can understand the attitude of hon. members from Ontario in regard to this matter because of the question of provincial rights. Naturally they have their attention fixed upon their constituencies; naturally they know what the people in their constituencies want, and if it became a conflict between the Dominion and provincial interests the weight of their support would go in favour of maintaining provincial interests. That is an understandable position from the standpoint of hon. members from Ontario; but we in this House ought to emphasize the interests of the Dominion. If there is a conflict between the interests of the Dominion of Canada and those of Ontario or Quebec, we should attach some importance to the interests of the Dominion of Canada.
What then is the situation? This is a measure which proposes to deal with a great internal waterway, a waterway that for three centuries has been a highway of commerce and traffic between Montreal and the Rocky mountains. That is a highway which the Dominion of Canada is interested in preserving for the use of the Dominion, and that is something to which we as representatives of constituencies in this Dominion parliament ought to give attention. We cannot for a moment concede that the people of Ontario and Quebec are the only ones who are interested in this matter. We who represent other parts of the Dominion 'have also an interest in seeing that, Whatever jmay be done in the development of this waterway, the interests of the Dominion as a whole are protected.
We have heard a great deal during the course of the debate about legal decisions -that have been rendered in favour of the claims of the provinces. I do not know enough about law or court decisions to know just what those decisions are or how far they go in determining the various matters at issue, but there is in the British North America Act a section that 'would bear study. Section 92 deals with the exclusive powers of provincial legislatures, and in subsection 10 we find that these matters are within the exclusive jurisdiction of the province:
Local works and understakings other than such as are of the following classes:

a.	Lines of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs, and other works and undertakings connecting the province with any other or others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of the province:
b.	Lines of steamships between the province and any British or foreign country:

Georgian Bay Canal Company
Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for ' the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
Therefore this parliament has the power to declare this work to be for the general advantage of Canada. Whether that should be done or not, I am not at the present time arguing; but I just want to point out that as there undoubtedly is a conflict between provincial and Dominion interests in this matter, this parliament has the power to declare that this particular work is not a matter in which the provinces alone are concerned, but that it is or may be a work for the general advantage of the people of Canada. The provinces and the Dominion alike derive their powers from this British North America Act. I am not a lawyer, but I think it is clear that this section is worthy of consideration in this connection. The leader of the opposition, speaking of the powers that lay within the jurisdiction of the province, made certain statements, but I notice that in section 91, which deals with the powers of parliament, subsection 12 includes "sea coast and inland fisheries." Therefore, when he declared that the fish in the stream belong to the provinces, that does not seem to me so absolutely beyond dispute unless some astute legal gentleman can show a distinction between fish and fisheries. Perhaps someone may be able to do that. We never know just how far astute legal arguments may carry. It would not at least seem to be so dear as hon. gentlemen have been endeavouring to assert, that the rights of the provinces are supreme in such matters as these.
Let us deal with the bill itself and I will try to state in terms that will not be misunderstood my attitude towards this question. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) produced the farmers' platform of Manitoba. I might as well confess that I had something to do with the preparation of that platform. I had the honour at the time of being president of the United Farmers of Manitoba and when we drew up that platform I was present. Indeed I am not sure that the particular clause referred to was not my own wording, and I . have no intention of departing from the position which I took then. I am opposed to the principle of this bill and I do not think it is possible to amend it in a way that would satisfy me. I think that is plain and definite enough for anybody.
What about the amendment? Technically, I admit that the amendment is correct. Undoubtedly the leader of the opposition when
he appealed to May, supported as he was by Bourinot, was correct in saying what he did in support of his amendment. I need not refer to his argument because it is well known. But while he is technically correct, it seems to me that the carrying of that amendment would not altogether meet the needs of the situation, because in my judgment it would leave unsettled a very important matter, a matter with which I think this House ought to deal promptly. The carrying of that amendment, it is true, would, so far as this House is concerned, put the whole question for the time being to one side. If we were to think of that amendment only in its own terms and no further, I for my part would have no objection to voting for it, but I think we are under an obligation to look further. Since I have been in this House I have learned that it is sometimes just as well, if you can get somewhere near where you want to go, to forget technicalities. Therefore, at the risk of being charged with inconsistency, I propose to take the other course. I have no hope that this particular bill can be amended in any way that will suit my views. My hope, in sending this matter to the committee, would be that from that committee might come some constructive proposition that would help us to deal properly with a great national problem. Now, somebody may say that this is not the right way to do it. It may not be the best way, it may not be the only way, but it seems to me that it is at least a good way.
We have heard a great many statements from both sides of the House in regard to the various interests that are concerning themselves with this or a kindred project for the development of power at the Carillon falls. What the exact situation is we have not the privilege of knowing. I think it well that we should know just as soon as possible what the exact situation is, and it seems to me that that could be brought out if this matter were placed before a committee of this House. I have no objection whatever to the terms of the amendment, but its acceptance would prevent our giving immediate consideration to the question. The great problem before Canada to-day is how we are to develop these great natural resources so that the people will receive the maximum good therefrom. It is with the hope that we may be able to do something immediately to solve the problem that I would cast aside technicalities and allow this matter to be referred to the committee, where we can get further information and probably suggestions that would be helpful to us. For example, it might very well be

Georgian Bay Canal Company
suggested that at once parliament should declare this whole work to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. I am mot saying that that would be done, but it is a possibility. It might be that the committee would suggest an immediate conference between the Dominion and the provinces. It might be that half a dozen suggestions would be made to bring us at once to grips with the situation. I have confidence enough in the members of this House, and certainly in the group with which I am immediately associated, to know that they stand absolutely firm on the question of the public control and development and operation of this great natural work for the general good of the people. There need be no question in the mind of any person on that point.
Speaking for myself, I take the position that we should send this bill to the committee, only in the hope that from the committee will come some suggestion to enable us to settle the question in the interests of the Dominion, whose rights in this great waterway are paramount. We cannot allow the interests of navigation to be sacrificed. I do not think for a moment that in the immediate future such a canal will be built either by private parties or by the Dominion; but who can foresee the future, who can tell us what the condition will be fifty years hence? We do not know. Whatever step we do take we must see to it that the rights of the Dominion in this great inland waterway are not permanently sacrificed. The rights of the Dominion must be protected. At the same time we must, of course, give consideration to the rights of the provinces. It is quite possible, as I have said, that this can be best done by a conference between the Dominion authorities and the representatives of the provinces. I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that this could be so done as to secure the end that we have in view-that these great natural resources shall be preserved and developed in such a way as to secure the maximum benefit for the great mass of the common people of Canada.

I am not talking about the hon. member for South Toronto, but the hon. member for Ottawa, and to-day he made exactly the statement I am making now. He drew a political line, and my hon. friend (Mr. Brown) tried to get away from that line, to hedge around it, or craw1! under it, or something of that kind. In fact he did not know what position he took, but the position of the hon. member for Ottawa was plain and distinct. In the early part of his remarks he made it a political question. Later on he spoke about sanguinary purposes and so on, and tried to connect the name of my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) with certain organizations in favour of one or other of the parties who are lined against us in favour of this scheme. He wias not very successful, and after that he appealed to everybody generally. He appealed to the members of parliament, the members from Quebec, the members from Montreal, and after he had made that distinct appeal to those members whom he knew were unfavourable to this canal project, or any other canal project for that matter, he appealed to the members from the west, and the only rise he got was from the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown)-the only member who would support him at this time.
When I spoke on this question previously I said without any equivocation that I believed this matter should go to the committee, the reason being that I believed in the canal. But I do not believe in the company. I have perfect faith in the canal scheme. I have no knowledge for or against the company which is behind the proposition at the present time. I have no reason to know, nor have I any reason to believe, that any set of parties, whether they be Siftons or Holts, are behind the proposition, and I do not care whether thej' are or not. All we ask is certain safeguards, and we can go along regardless of who may be behind the company. We believe that if any power is developed in the process of constructing the canal along the Ottawa river or the Frenoh river, or any portion of either or both of them, that power shall be under the control, eus to its distribution and price, of the Hydro Electric Commission, or of such other body as is appointed
by the province of Ontario, so far as Ontario rights are concerned. We believe equally that any power generated which belongs to the province of Quebec should be under the control of some body appointed by that province as to exportation or as to price.
The people of northern Ontario are absolutely in favour of this canal. They do not care anything about the power proposition, nor are they concerned with the company. As a matter of fact this canal project has been before the country for many years. The bill now under consideration is to all intents and purposes, according to parliamentary rules, one of a private nature, although I would point out to the ministry and particularly to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that it is not a private bill in the ordinary sense of the word. The charter has been opposed by Quebec and Ontario, the only two provinces in the Dominion that are interested in the matter; and the bill is being opposed likewise. This is consequently a government question on which the government should say either yes or no. They should be prepared to state whether they are ready to dispose of any of the rights that they may have in any or all of the streams, international or interprovincial, running through this country, or whether they are going to allow any or all companies to have charter rights along those streams. And the number of international and interprovincial streams in Canada are very few, and this is one of them. I have no doubt that the average man in Ontario and Quebee is awaiting a pronouncement from the government to the effect I suggest, but the only information we have had from the ministerial side comes from the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), who declares in favour of submitting the bill to the committee-for what purpose? To pass it? I think not. I think the government is tiying in a quiet and easy way to kill the bill or, in other words, to have an opportunity of disposing of this power without the interference of this particular company.
For many years practically all of the provinces were in favour of this canal. Speaking for Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec and the eastern provinces generally, I think it was the Consensus that this canal should be built: first, on the ground that it is all Canadian; secondly, that it would be over 300 miles shorter than the projected St. Lawrence route; thirdly, that it was cheaper to build; and in the fourth place- this is a secondary consideration-that it would not be affected by the levels of the great lakes. Originally the canal was projected on the basis of a nine-foot depth, to

Georgian Bay Canal Company
be built by the Georgian Bay Canal Company, and the next proposition was put forward, not by the canal company but by the Canadian Pacific Railway, who made complete survey of the French river section of the canal. I believe that had it not been for their financial condition at that time they would have 'built the canal on the basis of a sixteen-foot depth from the mouth of the French river to North Bay. We must bear in mind that when this proposition was put forward there was no such place as Cobalt. When the Canadian Pacific Railway were about to undertake the building of this section of the canal there was in northern Ontario no mining country of any description: Cobalt was entirely unknown and the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway had not even been projected. Indeed, even after the originally proposed depth had been increased to twenty or twenty-two feet our great paper mills of northern Ontario, which to-day are producing the greater proportion of our paper exports, had not been contemplated.
The government of Canada, under the administration of the present Prime Minister's predecessor, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, had a survey made of the whole canal proposition from one end to the other, although the report was submitted after that government had gone out of power. During their regime, however, a commission was appointed to look into the matter, and that commission afterwards reported. The commission cost Canada approximately one and a quarter million dollars and their report was that the canal scheme was absolutely feasible in every way. Nay, more, they said that there was not the slightest doubt that there would be plenty of water not only for the present but for the future. The building of the canal was delayed in many ways. In the first place there was the uncertainty as to capital; and, secondly, notwithstanding the favourable report of the commission, nothing could be done on account of the war, which came on soon afterwards. Next, a proviso was embodied in the charter whereby the government reserved the right to control this enterprise at all stages, so that no construction could be started until they agreed to the plans of the company. So far as I am aware these plans have never been agreed to by this or any other government. Another difficulty was this. After the government had taken away the power rights and had declared that all power generated should be at the disposal of the railway commission, and that no tolls should be charged on the canal, the company naturally asked for a guarantee of their bonds at three per cent; and this being refused, no construction has taken place.
IMr. Arthurs.]
Many of us on this side of the House were more or less opposed to the building of the present or the prospective Welland canal. The Welland canal now in course of construction was proposed by a government of which I was a humble follower, and the engineers' estimate was $50,000,000. We have already spent approximately $110,000,000 on that canal and the only result is that we are benefiting or will benefit ports on the American side. We have on the Canadian side no harbours which can receive boats of the capacity of the new Welland canal. The harbour of Toronto accommodates vessels of about sixteen feet, Cobourg, of about eleven feet, and so on along the lakes. The fact is that all deep water channels are along the other side of lake Ontario. Now, I believe the St. Lawrence oanal scheme is a good thing, and I have nothing against it. But Why should we not build from the ocean up? Why spend $110-
000.000 on the Welland canal when it is estimated that $108,000,000 would build canals up to lake Ontario? Our eastern friends can bring up their coal gradually ns the canals are built into the province of Ontario, but if you start at the Welland canal and work down the inevitable result will be that their American competitors will follow the canals mile by mile, and instead of getting coal or other products from Nova Scotia we in Ontario will find that American trade is using that canal.
I would also like to call the attention of the government to a very important point in connection with this proposition. It is all very well to sit back and say, we are going to build the Welland canal, or the St. Lawrence system or some other canal, at a cost of $500,000,000 or $800,000,000 or $1,400,000,000; the same proposition will come up in each case. Where are you going to get the water and how are you going to get the harbours? Our friends from Montreal know very well that there is very serious danger to the ship channel between Montreal and the ocean; they know that even there the level is being lowered. I hold in my hand a return of this House under date of February 28, in answer to a question as to what action the government had taken to ascertain the levels of the various lakes, and also to inquire what action had been taken in regard to a protest or claim at Washington. In answer to that we are told that the lowering of the level in lake Huron due to the Chicago drainage canal has been 0.5 feet, and that the lowering of the level due to the removal of gravel from lake St. Clair was 0.6 feet, or in all a lowering of 1.1 feet. I was not satisfied with that answer and asked a question later in this

Again they admit provincial rights, but before they get through they throw provincial rights to the winds in the following:
Therefore the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian bay canal have the exclusive and overriding right to the use of water on the Ottawa river, a right which, when put into force, destroys all other claims. But notice the qualification:
To the extent to which they interfere with the rights of development and control of that river for navigation.

condemns itself. I wish all hon. gentlemen had secured copies of it, for I have no doubt that if they had read it there would have been removed from their minds any doubt whatever as to the proper action this parliament should take in respect to the bill now under consideration: they would reject it ruthlessly.
There is another point to be considered. The hon. member who has just taken his seat, (Mr. Arthurs) made a 'brief reference to it and I may mention it once more because it is one of the strongest arguments against the charter. Surely Canada has had sufficient lessons in the duplication of transportation systems. Surely we have been cured of the mania for grasping at visionary plans of promoters and allowing them to secure public property with a view to realizing some extraordinary ambitious grandiose scheme of transportation. The lessons we have .learned with respect to our Canadian transcontinental lines should have convinced us forever of the danger of grasping too easily at such projects. A few years ago we started the Welland canal in which we have sunk nearly $100,000,000 and it will cost the country another twenty to twenty-five million dollars, and possibly more to complete that undertaking. Now if we assume, although I am not willing to do so, except for the sake of argument, that every statement made is correct in relation to the possibility of constructing the canal now under consideration, that the canal can be built to serve a useful purpose, that it will secure the mass of tonnage which the brief of the promoters alleges it will, then I have this to say, that it would take away from the Welland canal project the last possible hope of salvaging one dollar of the taxpayers' money invested in this project for it would then completely replace that canal and render it useless. Are we still mad that we are going to commit ourselves to such a folly? Do we want to lose $110,000,000 already invested in a canal which is almost completed in order to satisfy the promoters of this charter?
Another reason given for the construction of this canal, rather than the completion of the Welland or the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway, is the possibility that in the future we may be faced with the horrors of a conflict with the United States. Georgian Bay Canal Company
That project will be commenced and completed just as soon as this country is ready for it, just as soon as the people want it and when we are prepared to undertake our share of the expense in connection with it. All through history and even to this moment, Mr. Speaker, this charter has been surrounded by the most sinister influences. I am now adopting, I will admit, some of the tactics of my hon. friend in referring to it in this way, but I am compelled to do so because many editorials have appeared recently referring to the extensive and highly efficient professional lobbying which has been carried on among members of this House. Personally I have no objection to a lobby if it is reasonable; I am glad to hear all sides of a question, but when a lobbyist comes to my room, as a rule he simply incites my curiosity and causes me to seek information in other places. Very well. I have in my hand an editorial appearing in the Catholic Record of London, Ontario, under date of Saturday, March 19. With reference to the sale of royal honours in Great Britain, this editorial says:
Campaign funds are perhaps a necessary evil.
Stable government, with an assured majority, is a good thing. But a government with an 32649-90J
assured majority may do things that a government with a precarious majority would not dare to do.
After all, while the sale of royal honours may muddy up the fountain of honour, it does not cost the common people anything. It is a distasteful way of raising party funds, but it is not stealing from the people.
There are men in public life who would scorn to enrich themselves by dishonest or /dishonourable means, but who would not hesitate to buy campaign funds with the gift of public property.	_
Just now in Canada there is the question of reviving the old dead and buried Georgian bay canal.
There is one and only one reason for this revival.
It is party funds.
A stable government, with an assured majority, may look to this source of party funds and dally with it; perhaps put over this gift of electric power to private interests under the pretence of constructing a canal for the benefit of the people. But not if the people show themselves alive to their own interests.
It would be ten thousand times worse than the sale of royal honours. There is no reason in the world for such a shameless transaction other than the necessity of raising party funds. And to rob the people in order to pay the pirates who will contribute to party funds is infinitely worse than to sell royal honours for cash.
Along with that, we had an incident which occurred during the life of this charter not so many years ago. The House suddenly discovered, after it had passed the bill, that the bill before the Senate was not the bill which had been passed by the House. Something had happened to it in the meantime, some sinister influence had been at work, and the major part of the framework of the bill had been altered. Let me quote from Hansard of February 20, 1913, at page 3741, where Mr. Lancaster, then chairman of the committee on railways and canals moved, seconded by M|r. White of Renfrew, the following:
That a message be sent to the Senate requesting their honours to return to this House Bill No. 45, respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company, as it appears that the said bill as sent to the Senate is not printed as passed by the House of Commons.
Some members asked him to explain, and he proceeded as follows:
It has come to my notice that their honours in the Senate will be called upon to consider a bill presumably passed by this House, but which, if considered in its present form, would put this' House in a very ridiculous position. The House of Commons, after due deliberation, passed the bill referred to, and section 4 of the bill as sent to the Senate undertakes to repeal the whole of chapter 123 of the statutes of 1912. This House never did any such thing. It was never suggested by any member that we should. What we did was to repeal section 1. In some strange way-I do not want to impute motives, but I have to have a good deal of

Georgian Bay Canal Company
charity in my disposition to think this interference was not intentional-after the House dealt with the bill the bill was printed in such a way as to strike out the whole chapter instead of what the House actually did. The effect would be that the company would have no directors and provincial rights with regard to water-powers would not be protected. It is a strange thing; the House will have to deal with it afterwards as they see fit, but it is my duty now as chairman of the railway committee of the House of Commons to call attention to the fact that this House has been placed in the position of having sent a bill to the Senate which we never passed as sent, and I move that the Senate be asked to send that bill back to us in order that a proper bill as passed by this House may go to them for consideration.
This motion was agreed to unanimously. Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to delay the House very much longer in this connection. I do submit, however, that this charter should not be renewed for many reasons, first perhaps because of the utter failure of the company to even file plans that could be accepted, the utter failure of the company to do the least thing in keeping with recommendations of the engineers of the Department of Public Works. The company have had thirty-two years in which to do this and nothing has been done as yet. And then again, there is the engineering feature of the scheme. I will be as kind as possible to my friends opposite, but the very best that can be said is that there are grave doubts of the feasibility of this canal scheme, and in any case let me submit what I said before, that if the canal is found to be feasible it should be undertaken as a national enterprise by the Dominion government, and not by a private corporation. Again, the granting of this charter would be a violation of the principle of public ownership, and of the control of the provinces over their own water-powers. The statements of the promoters which I have just read prove conclusively that as soon. as the charter is granted they will assume, by virtue of the overriding right vested in the Dominion government, and surrendered to the company to complete and utter control of every interest located along the canal which may- interfere with their own project. Again it violates the principle of toll-free canals, and interferes with the development of national ownership of our waterways. It would place at the mercy of an utterly merciless corporation-a private group of some notoriety, which has not public interest as its guiding influence-all those users of electrical power in the immediate vicinity of these works. Any reasonably-minded man knows that the objectives of a commercial corporation such as that seeking this charter are not altruistic and that they are not work-
ing for the good of the people. Commercialism to-day has become too bitter for that; it is too vicious a system to ever grant to the people justice and equality. It would place at the disposal of private interests a heritage of the people, and would subject those people in the immediate vicinity of the canal almost to a condition of subjugation in connection with the power for use in the factories and mills and on the farms of the district. It goes to the length of suggesting that those who use power should pay for what should be a national avenue of transportation. That, perhaps, is one of the most vicious features of the whole proposal. It will in the opinion of the hydro-electric commission, according to the statement of Mr. Magrath, and I believe the statement to be perfectly true, prejudice the whole future of hydro development in the province of Ontario. Let us not forget that the hydro-electric commission has reached the limit of its present development, and for its future expansion there are only two great sources of water-power left. One is the St. Lawrence, and the time may not have arrived when we can undertake that development, and the other is the Ottawa river. Do we propose to stop the expansion of public ownership in Ontario by granting to private interests their half-and I say it with all my belief behind it-of the rights to the water-powers of the Ottawa river? Shall we prejudice the whole future of hydroelectric and with that the whole principle of public ownership in the province; to do so would be an indefensible flouting of the expressed, the unanimously expressed, will of the province of Ontario; it would be a flouting of the expressed desire of the province of Quebec through the mouth of its own premier, and it would destroy the last vestige of hope left to the shareholders in the nation, the taxpayers, of securing one dollar back out of the enormous investment of one hundred and twenty millions to which we are committed in the Welland canal.
For all these reasons, and for other reasons which I do not wish to delay the House in reciting, I am opposed to the granting of this charter. I am opposed to this bill even going to committee, because no committee can change the principles under which this charter is being sought. Why waste the valuable time of members of this House by asking them to investigate a bill the underlying principles of which are in violation of the recognized principles I have referred to? That Would be stupid and futile. It would be stupid to let a bill, the fundamentals of which

Georgian Bay Canal Company
you could not change, go to a committee and be killed there. Hon. members opposite have said: Jet it go to committee and we will kill it there. Why waste time talking over this bill for a couple of months just to kill it in committee? Kill it now. The principle of the bill is unsound, absolutely unsound in every respect. Whether as regards the canal development or as regards the power development, it is unsound in principle. It is a violation of the rights of the people. It is a clear, absolute and complete theft of the people's property. It is a deliberate attempt to surrender the heritage of the Canadian people to private interests. subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I
intend to take very little time this evening in discussing the amendment to this bill to renew the charter of the Montreal and Georgian Bay Canal Company. To begin with I am opposed to the bringing into effect of the legislation sought by this measure, because I believe that such a move will alienate the rights of the Canadian people as regards water-power and other rights on the Ottawa river, and other rivers concerned. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) stated during his remarks the other night that this was a fight between two rival companies for the. control of the power at Carillon. I trust, Mr. Speaker, that before this debate is ended the people of this country will, through their representatives in this House, claim those rights for themselves, that they will claim what the Minister of Railways told us was the bone of contention, namely, the power on the Ca/rillon falls.
In common with the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Garland, Bow River) I believe the big question under discussion to-night is not one of allotting power rights to certain interests. The whole question is: are we for or against public ownership? I believe that there is a movement on foot to-day to monopolize to a great extent the available hydro-electric energy in this Dominion. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) pointed out in his admirable address quite clearly that two or three groups of financial interests controlled the hydro-electric energy in Canada to such an extent that their income almost equals that of the Canadian National Railways, or the total income of the province of Ontario. The control of electrical energy in this country to-day will, I contend, mean the
absolute control of the industrial life .of the country before many years have gone by, and with the rapid advance in the development of electrical service .that day is steadily drawing nearer. The question, therefore, which faces the people of Canada to-day is: shall they control Ithe power, or shall the power interests control them?
In the constituency which I have the honour to represent is developed all the hydro-electric energy used in the province of Manitoba, and the history of the circumstances surrounding the entry of the city of Winnipeg into the hydro business is one which would convince anybody who happens to live within that vicinity of the advantages of public ownership over private control. Before the city of Winnipeg went into the hydro-electric business they were paying 20 cents per kilowatt hour for the power used in that city. Immediately following the building of their plant at Pointe de Bois the price of power dropped to 10 cents, and to-day it is only three cents, which goes to show the advantages of a publicly owned utility.
As an example of the monopolies existing in certain parts of the United States I should just like to quote one or two facts. On July 25, 1925 it was announced that the Middle West Utilities Company had perfected mergers and consolidations that gave control of public utility services in 1,269 cities, towns and villages in 18 different states. In other words the public service utilities in 18 different states, and in 1,269 towns, were at the absolute mercy of a private corporation. This question of the monopoly of electrical energy is one that is engaging the most serious attention of the nation just south of the international border. It is engaging their attention because of the fact that they have awakened, when it is too late, to find that they are at the merey of the power interests in that country. In this connection may I quote what Governor Clifford Pinchot, of Pennsylvania, in his message of transmittal of the report of his Giant Power Survey Board, made public in February, 1925, had to say regarding the power trust in the United States. Speaking of the power trust he says:
Nothing like this gigantic monopoly has ever appeared in the history of the world. Nothing has ever been imagined before that, even remotely approaches it in the thoroughgoing, intimate, unceasing control it may exercise over the daily life of every human being within the web of its wires'. It is immeasurably the greatest industrial fact of our time. If uncontrolled, it will be a plague without previous example. If effectively controlled in the public interest, it can be made incomparably the greatest material blessing in human history.

Georgian Bay Canal Company
That is the opinion of the governor of one of the largest states in the American union after a thorough investigation had been made by a committee. Senator Norris, who has filled page after page of the congressional record with facts regarding this trust, states that he has been dumbfounded and amazed to learn that over twenty millions out of fifty-five millions horse-power of potential hydroelectric power in the United States have been already awarded to or applied for by private organizations.
I notice in a Washington paper dated March 19 of this year an article on the power situation as it affects the United States. It is headed "Federal Commission discloses how small group dominates electric field", and it reads:
Responding to a resolution introduced by Senator Norris of Nebraska, asking information on the power trust and its interests in Muscle shoals, the Federal Trade Commission has made a report which more than justifies every warning of monopoly uttered by Senator Norris and Senator Walsh of Montana.
It shows that a little group of interests controls almost 90 per cent of the power development of this country, that these interests are interlocked, and that the profits make Croesus look like a piker.
Owing to the holding device, the concentration of power is almost unbelievable.
"In one instance," the commission says, "less than a million dollar investment in the majority of the voting stock of the apex holding company gave full control of the entire organization of the group, having scores of underlying companies and several hundred million dollars of investment."
Another item appearing in a New York paper under date of March 14 of this year states:
Power Issue Splits Smith and "G.O.P." N.Y. Republican Leaders Favour "Private Enterprise" Against "Government Control" New York, March 14.-The long expected break between Governor "Al" Smith and the Republican organization which controls both branches of the state legislature has developed.
The governor insists that New York's waterpower resources must be developed under state control.
That is what the Governor of New York state says about the matter:
The Republican leaders are determined that the power trust shall have a chance to do the job.
The G.O.P. leaders propose to name a commission to study the hydro-electric problem, with authority to consider both public and private development. Governor Smith maintains that the inquiry should be confined to the feasibility of public development.
The result will probably be a deadlock of indefinite duration.

The power trust is willing to permit things to remain as they are. It hopes that Smith will go out of office in 1928 and that he will be succeeded by someone who is more favourable to the trust.
Those two items dated only this month give quite a clear idea of what the power situation is in two of the largest states in the great union just south of us and show that it is a problem which is engaging the earnest attention of many at the head of public affairs in both of those states.
As I stated a few minutes ago, and I think, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy), in his address the other day, suggested it, the control of electrical energy represents in great measure the control o-f the development of the industrial life of the country. I notice that in the city of Chicago 45 per cent, in Indiana 60 per cent, and in Ontario 85 per cent of the industrial plants use cheap electrical energy for their operation.
Why, may I ask, are so many branch factories of United States manufacturing concerns coming to Canada to-day? Some hon. gentleman would say: because of the tariff. Whatever relation the tariff may have to the question of building up industries in Ontario, I believe the real answer is the hydro electric system of that province. In support of that statement, I might state that in the hearings before the Senate committee of the United States on the Fordney-McCumber tariff bill, the chamber of commerce of Niagara Falls, New York, presented a memorial in which it is stated that the manufacturers of Ontario enjoy a power rate of one-half of that which is charged by the privately owned corporations of the state of New York, and therefore it prays for tariff rates to protect them from the competition of Ontario manufacturers. It will be seen from this that cheap hydro electric power is a greater factor in the industrial life of the country than probably any other single factor. I think these figures will demonstrate the advantages which have accrued to many municipalities and cities by taking over this hydro-electrical development. I contend that the organization, unification and inter-connection of vast and far-reaching electrical power systems are inevitable for the reasons which I have already briefly pointed out. We are coming more and more face to face with that self-same situation. The economic advantages to be gained by such a system are so great that, whether we like it or not, we are rapidly being drawn into it. The question which this country has to face to-day is this: Shall this be a private or a public monopoly? For that reason I contend that the bill under discussion means nothing more nor less than this: Are we going to hand over to private interests the potential electrical energy of the great waterways of Canada, or are we going to see that they remain and are controlled and developed for the general advantage of the people of this country. Because I believe the water rights of this country should be retained, owned and controlled by the Dominion of Canada for the general benefit of the citizens thereof, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward):
That all the words after the word " therefor " in the said amendment be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
That inasmuch as the construction of the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian bay canal and the development of the water-powers incident thereto are essentially of the nature of public utilities,
That these undertakings, including the development of all works for water-powers or others, on the Ottawa river, Mattawa river and French river, if not within the class of works which have been declared for the general advantage of Canada or the advantage of two or more provinces under the statute of 1870, shall be so declared.
That in the opinion of this House such natural resources should not be alienated,
And also, that no further leases or extensions of leases on the Ottawa river, Mattawa river and French river should be granted without the consent of parliament.	[DOT]
That all existing rights, claims and leases in private hands, as affecting the Ottawa river, Mattawa river and French river, with the exception of those power sites already fully developed, should be recovered for the general benefit of the people of Canada,
And further, that this House is of the opinion that the developments on the Ottawa river, Mattawa river and French river should be taken over by the government of Canada as part of a comprehensive scheme for the supplying of navigation facilities and hydroelectric power to the people of the Dominion of Canada at the lowest possible cost.
